lead: At Lystra a crowd takes two missionaries for gods, and Paul and Barnabas rush in among the people to stop the sacrifice. In the Gospel Jesus promises that the Father and he will come and make their home with those who love him, and that the Holy Spirit will teach and remind. Psalm 115 answers both: glory belongs not to us but to the Lord’s name, and the idols of silver and gold are only the work of human hands.

r.h: We are mortals just like you
set: This is the first missionary journey of Paul and Barnabas (chapters 13–14), sent out by the church of Antioch in Syria (13:1–3). After Pisidian Antioch and Iconium, a threat of stoning drives them on to Lystra and Derbe, towns of Lycaonia in the south of present-day Turkey. Augustus had made Lystra a Roman colony, but the ordinary people spoke their own Lycaonian language.

Background. The Roman poet Ovid tells an old tale of Jupiter and Mercury (Zeus and Hermes, in Greek) visiting the neighbouring region of Phrygia in human form, unrecognised by everyone except one old couple. Many commentators think a local story of this kind explains why the crowd was so quick to see gods in the two strangers.
str: vv. 5–7: the plot at Iconium and the flight to Lystra and Derbe.
vv. 8–10: a man lame from birth is healed.
vv. 11–13: the crowd cries out that the gods have come; the priest of Zeus prepares a sacrifice.
vv. 14–18: Barnabas and Paul tear their clothes and speak of the living God.
kw: The crowd shouts in its local tongue, which Paul and Barnabas probably did not understand. This may be why they react only when the oxen and garlands arrive (v. 14).
Empty, vain things. The Greek Old Testament uses this kind of word for idols. Paul calls the people away from what cannot give life to the God who does.
“Mortals just like you” (v. 15): people with the same weakness. James 5:17 uses the same word of Elijah. The apostles will not let a miracle make them more than human.
vv: And Paul, looking at him intently and seeing that he had faith to be healed,
Luke tells this healing much like Peter’s healing of the man lame from birth at the Temple gate, where Peter too “looked intently” at him (3:4). The same Lord works through both apostles.
“Stand upright on your feet.” And the man sprang up and began to walk.
No name is invoked aloud here, but the sermon he had just heard was about Jesus. Faith came by hearing, and healing followed.
We are mortals just like you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these worthless things to the living God,
Tearing one’s clothes was a Jewish sign of horror at blasphemy. The greatest danger for a preacher is to be worshipped. Paul and Barnabas turn every eye away from themselves.
yet he has not left himself without a witness in doing good
To people who did not know the Scriptures, Paul begins with rain, harvest, food and joy. Creation itself speaks of the Creator.
ch: This is the first speech in Acts to a purely pagan audience, and it begins not from the prophets but from creation, as Paul will do again in Athens (17:22–31). The Church teaches that God can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason (CCC 36, from the First Vatican Council). She rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions (Nostra Aetate 2), and like Paul and Barnabas she will never let a creature, however gifted, take the place of the living God.

r.h: We will make our home with them
set: We are at the Last Supper. One after another the disciples interrupt with questions: Peter (13:36), Thomas (14:5), Philip (14:8), and now Judas, “not Iscariot”. Luke calls him Judas son of James (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13), and tradition identifies him with Thaddeus (Mark 3:18). The Church honours him with St Simon on 28 October.
str: v. 21: love is proved by keeping his commandments, and he will reveal himself.
v. 22: Judas asks why to them and not to the world.
vv. 23–24: the answer: the Father and the Son will come and dwell.
vv. 25–26: the Advocate will teach and remind.
kw: The same word as the “dwelling places” of the Father’s house in 14:2. There, we go to dwell with God; here, God comes to dwell with us. The Father’s house begins now in the heart that loves.
Literally one called to stand beside someone: a helper, a defender, a comforter. In 1 John 2:1 the same word is used of Jesus himself; in John 14:16 the Spirit is “another Advocate”.
The Spirit will bring back to mind all that Jesus said. The Gospels themselves are fruit of this remembering.
vv: Lord, how is it that you will reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?
Judas perhaps expected a public triumph. Jesus answers by speaking of love, not of display.
Those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them.
Not a passing visit but a home. The whole Trinity dwells in the one who loves: the Father, the Son, and, as the next verses say, the Spirit.
will teach you everything, and remind you of all that I have said to you.
The Spirit does not bring a new Gospel. He makes the one Gospel understood and alive in every age.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 23 when it says that the goal of God’s whole plan is that his creatures enter the perfect unity of the Blessed Trinity, who already now come to dwell in us (CCC 260). It explains that Paraclete means “he who is called to one’s side” (CCC 692), and it calls the Holy Spirit the Church’s living memory (CCC 1099).

qa: Why did the Risen Jesus not show himself to the whole world?

In Acts Peter says that God allowed him to appear not to all the people but to witnesses chosen beforehand (Acts 10:40–41). God does not force himself on anyone. He shows himself to those who love and keep his word, and through their witness he reaches the world.
study: Where am I tempted to take credit for what God has done, as the crowd at Lystra wanted to give it to Paul and Barnabas?
If the Father and the Son make their home in me, what in my daily life would I want to tidy, and what would I want to open?
